
---
title: "Research"
---

My research investigates the physical processes governing energy transfer
and particle energization in weakly collisional plasmas. The solar wind
provides an extraordinary natural laboratory for this work, allowing
spacecraft observations to be compared directly with predictions from
plasma theory and numerical simulations.

Our work combines analytical theory, numerical modeling, and observations
from missions including Parker Solar Probe, Solar Orbiter, and Wind.
Three interconnected areas form the foundation of this research.

## Turbulence and plasma heating

How does turbulent energy move across scales, and which physical processes
ultimately transfer that energy to particles?

We study turbulent cascades, intermittency, kinetic-scale fluctuations,
and the connections between spatial structure and collisionless energy
transfer. A central objective is to identify the mechanisms responsible
for plasma heating and determine how their relative importance changes
across different plasma environments.

### Highlighted publications

**[Evidence for electron Landau damping in space plasma turbulence](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-019-08435-3)**  
*Chen, Klein & Howes (2019), Nature Communications.*

Using spacecraft measurements of electromagnetic fields and electron
velocity distributions, we identified a velocity-space signature
consistent with electron Landau damping in turbulent plasma. This
demonstrates how field–particle correlations can directly constrain
collisionless energy-transfer mechanisms in space plasmas.


**[Mind the gap: non-local cascades and preferential heating in high-beta Alfvénic turbulence](https://doi.org/10.1093/mnrasl/slae018)**  
*Gorman & Klein (2024), Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society: Letters.*

We investigate how nonlocal interactions in Alfvénic turbulence
influence the transfer of energy across scales and its redistribution
between particle species. This work connects the properties of
turbulent energy cascades to preferential heating in high-beta
plasma environments.

## Kinetic plasma physics

Space plasmas often depart strongly from local thermodynamic
equilibrium, exhibiting temperature anisotropies, relative drifts,
and non-Maxwellian particle velocity distributions.

We investigate how these departures influence wave propagation,
kinetic instabilities, and wave–particle energy exchange.
Numerical dispersion tools and spacecraft measurements provide
complementary constraints on the stability and evolution of
collisionless plasmas.

### Highlighted publications

**[Majority of Solar Wind Intervals Support Ion-Driven Instabilities](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.121.045101)****  
*Klein et al. (2018), Physical Review Letters.*

By applying linear kinetic stability analysis to measured solar-wind
ion distributions, we demonstrated that a majority of sampled
intervals support ion-driven instabilities. This work established
the importance of considering the combined effects of multiple
ion populations, temperature anisotropies, and differential flows
when assessing plasma stability.

**[The dielectric response of plasmas with arbitrary gyrotropic
velocity distributions](https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0286477)**  
*Klein & Verscharen (2025), Physics of Plasmas.*

We develop methods for evaluating the kinetic dielectric response
of plasmas with arbitrary gyrotropic velocity distributions, including
the treatment of resonances through analytic continuation.
These advances expand the range of realistic particle distributions
that can be investigated using numerical dispersion solvers such
as ALPS.

## Multi-spacecraft measurements and heliophysics missions

Multi-point spacecraft observations provide new ways to distinguish
spatial from temporal variability, characterize turbulent structure,
and reconstruct gradients in evolving plasmas.

I am Deputy Principal Investigator of NASA's HelioSwarm mission and
Project Scientist for the SWEAP investigation aboard Parker Solar
Probe. A central component of our work is developing and validating
the measurement strategies and analysis methods needed to extract
three-dimensional plasma physics from distributed spacecraft
observations.

### Highlighted publications

**[HelioSwarm: A Multipoint, Multiscale Mission to Characterize
Turbulence](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11214-023-01019-0)**  
*Klein et al. (2023), Space Science Reviews.*

We describe the scientific motivation and measurement strategy
of NASA's nine-spacecraft HelioSwarm mission. By simultaneously
sampling plasma fluctuations across multiple spatial separations,
HelioSwarm will enable measurements of three-dimensional turbulent
structure, intermittency, and multiscale energy transfer that are
inaccessible to traditional single-spacecraft observations.


**[Wave-Telescope Analysis for Multipoint Observatories: Impact of Timing and Spatial Uncertainties](https://doi.org/10.1029/2024JA033428)**  
*Klein, Broeren, Roberts & Schulz (2024), Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics.*

We investigate how spacecraft timing and position uncertainties
affect the reconstruction of spatial fluctuations using multipoint
wave-telescope analysis. This work helps establish the measurement
accuracy and analysis requirements needed to recover reliable
three-dimensional information from future multispacecraft missions.
